title: Four Eyes Good: The History of Glasses
summary: Josh and Chuck (the transcript labels one host as "iHeart Intro" in places) explore the history of eyeglasses, based on research by Livia. They cover why people needed corrective lenses before glasses existed, early magnifying and reading stones, ancient lenses used for fire-starting, Ibn al-Haytham's optics work and its transmission to Europe, early convex lenses in Italy, concave lenses for nearsightedness, Raphael's portrait of Pope Leo X, rivet spectacles, the bow spectacle, temple arms and the ear problem (Edward Scarlett, James Ice Coff), Martin's margins, 19th-century eye exams and the ophthalmoscope and ophthalmometer, the diopter, plastic lenses and the 1972 FDA shatterproof rule, WWI/WWII military glasses, bifocals and Ben Franklin, progressive lenses, monocles, sunglasses and photochromic transition lenses, NASA-derived scratch-resistant coatings, contact lenses, and modern eyeglass statistics. The episode ends with a listener letter from Lucy in Canada praising respectful transgender language.

segments.title: Opening banter about glasses
segments.summary: The hosts joke about wearing glasses, their first pairs, and the social stigma and fashion of glasses over time.

segments.title: Why people needed glasses before glasses were invented
segments.summary: Discussion of how reading increased myopia and the need for corrective lenses, and that people who could not see far or near were less noticed before widespread reading.

segments.title: Ancient lenses and early magnification
segments.summary: Ancient people ground quartz into lenses about five thousand years ago, used for starting fires, with independent development in Assyria, Greece and Peru. The hosts mention Archimedes' burning mirror and a prior episode on mirrors.

segments.title: Ibn al-Haytham, optics, and monks translating texts
segments.summary: Ibn al-Haytham showed that eyes sense light beams, a view later translated into Latin by Vitelo and built on by Roger Bacon. Reading stones let monks magnify text.

segments.title: Early convex lenses in Italy and Germany
segments.summary: Convex lenses for farsightedness developed in late thirteenth-century Italy, with Nicholas of Kusa credited in Germany. Florence crafted high-quality lenses.

segments.title: Rivet spectacles and the Gutenberg printing boom
segments.summary: Rivet spectacles were early hinged glasses held by a rivet, still without arms. Reading spread with the Gutenberg press and newspapers, increasing demand for glasses. Glasses were held by hand for centuries; the medieval fashion question arose.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break between segments.

segments.title: Velma joke and transition
segments.summary: Banter about Velma from Scooby-Doo saying 'my glasses' and the Arabic name pronunciation.

segments.title: Concave lenses for nearsightedness and Raphael's portrait
segments.summary: Concave lenses for nearsightedness came in the fifteenth century. Raphael's portrait of Pope Leo X shows a concave lens, and the Medici family had myopia.

segments.title: Glass improvements, bow spectacles, and temple arms
segments.summary: Seventeenth-century additions such as lead oxide and potash raised refractive index, making lenses thinner. Bow spectacles rested on the nose. Edward Scarlett invented temples in London in the 1720s; they pressed on the temples because wigs covered the ears. Ice Coff's hinged temples followed.

segments.title: Hinged temples and sunglasses tastes
segments.summary: Hinged, spring temples let glasses fit different head sizes. The hosts discuss modern sunglass shapes and visor sunglasses.

segments.title: Napoleon's glasses and Martin's margins
segments.summary: Napoleon reportedly refused glasses for appearance and was clumsy as a result. Benjamin Martin invented thick-rimmed Martin's margins, which blocked light from above and below and became fashionable.

segments.title: Nineteenth-century eye exams and the ophthalmoscope
segments.summary: Traveling salesmen sold ready-made spectacles before the 19th century. Herman von Helmholtz invented the ophthalmoscope and ophthalmometer in the 1850s, enabling custom prescriptions. The French ophthalmologists of the 1870s established the diopter.

segments.title: Diopters and modern eye exams
segments.summary: The diopter quantifies the refraction correction needed. The hosts discuss how eye exams work, including the phoropter-like machine and the air puff test.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts announce a break before talking about plastics, bifocals, monocles and sunglasses.

segments.title: Plastic lenses, FDA shatterproof rule, and military glasses
segments.summary: After World War I, resin CR-39 became a popular lens plastic. In 1972 the FDA required shatterproof lenses in the US, pushing makers toward plastics. The World Wars spurred military glasses, nicknamed birth control glasses.

segments.title: Bifocals and progressive lenses
segments.summary: Ben Franklin described bifocals in a letter by having glassmakers cut two pairs of glasses in half. Progressive lenses came in 1959 and are multifocal.

segments.title: Monocles and sunglasses history
segments.summary: Monocles signaled wealth and pomposity; women in early-twentieth-century Weimar Germany used them as a fashion statement. Inuit sun goggles and Samuel Pepys' tinted glasses are mentioned, plus a legend about Nero and emeralds.

segments.title: Photochromic and transition lenses
segments.summary: Transition lenses are a trademarked type of photochromic lens. The dyes darken with UV exposure and clear indoors; the hosts discuss how it works and credit Warby Parker for an explanation.

segments.title: Scratch-resistant lenses and NASA technology
segments.summary: Scratch-resistant coatings for plastic lenses came from NASA technology licensed by Foster Grant in 1983. Scratch resistance made glasses last much longer.

segments.title: Contact lenses history and disposables
segments.summary: Contacts debuted in 1887 as glass lenses. Soft contacts came in the 1960s. The hosts discuss disposable and multifocal contacts and sleeping in them.

segments.title: Modern eyeglass statistics and wrap-up
segments.summary: Statistics: about 166 million US adults wear prescription eyeglasses, about 34.5 million use over-the-counter readers, and about 45 million wear contacts. The hosts close the main topic.

segments.title: Listener mail from Lucy in Canada
segments.summary: Lucy thanks the hosts for respectfully referring to a transgender child, and the hosts respond with thanks and a reminder about sending mail.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Standard show sign-off and production credit.
